meta.regime: The regime is a physical energy supply shock transmitting into the long end of the US curve, and yesterday it finally showed up there in a way nobody can ignore: the 10-year Treasury yield topped 5% for the first time since 2023 and closed at its highest level since 2007. That is the missing link this file has been circling for a week. It explains why gold fell on a day the Saudi bypass was shut, why the franc will not bid, why the dollar has risen four sessions running, and why an equity index like GER40 is now squeezed from two directions at once. The transmission is concrete rather than abstract: AAA has US pump gasoline at 4.31 dollars and diesel at a RECORD 6.23 dollars, and diesel is the input price for trucking, rail, farming and shipping, so the market is repricing not the oil shock itself but its pass-through into everything else. The second feature, and today's genuinely new one, is that this has pushed rate pricing PAST the Fed's own published projections. Futures carry two more quarter-point hikes by year-end against a June dot plot showing one, with FedWatch near 89% for Wednesday. For a month this file has treated the dot plot as a hawkish catalyst; it is now more accurately a dovish risk, because the committee has to move toward the market rather than the market toward the committee. The third feature is that the commodity split that has driven the cross-rate book is no longer widening. WTI added another 1.92% to 103.333 and Brent 1.76% to 107.545, but copper printed exactly 0.00% at 6.3303 after China's industrial production beat, and gold fell only 0.15% on the day the 10-year broke 5%. Energy is still bid, industrial metals stopped falling, and bullion is quietly refusing to break. Those three are the cracks to watch in a book that has been leaning on all three continuing.

dailyRead: The most important number on this page is not an FX rate. The US 10-year Treasury yield topped 5% yesterday for the first time since 2023 and closed at its highest level since 2007, driven by the energy shock rather than by growth, with AAA reporting pump gasoline at 4.31 dollars and diesel at a RECORD 6.23 dollars a gallon. That single move is the mechanism this file has been describing in fragments for a week. It is why gold fell 1.74% on Monday with the Saudi bypass shut, why the franc has failed three consecutive haven tests, why the dollar has now risen four sessions running to DXY 99.634, and why an equity index carrying European gas costs is squeezed from two sides at once. Naming the mechanism matters because it tells you what would break the book: not a peace headline, but a fall in US real yields. Now the uncomfortable part, and it cuts against the dollar longs this file has been running. Futures now price TWO more quarter-point hikes by year-end, and FedWatch for Wednesday has risen to roughly 89% from 86%. The Fed's own published projections, which TE carries explicitly, show 3.8% for the current year, then 3.6%, 3.4%, 3.1% and 3.1% longer-run - one more hike, then cuts. The market is therefore priced HAWKISH OF THE COMMITTEE'S OWN PATH. For a month this file has treated Wednesday's dot plot as a potential hawkish catalyst for the dollar. On today's pricing that is backwards: a dot plot that merely confirms the June profile is now a DOVISH surprise, because the burden has shifted to the Fed to move toward the market rather than the reverse. To satisfy pricing, Warsh's committee has to lift the current-year dot to 4.0% or above and flatten the out-years. That does not change today's positions - the board is unchanged and the dollar longs stay on - but it does change the risk around them, and it is why USD is held at +2 rather than raised, why USD/CAD stays LOW-MED rather than being pressed, and why every dollar ticket on this page now carries the same named invalidation. Second, no scores move today, and the two calls that could have moved are worth stating plainly because refusing to act is also a decision. JPY is NOT cut a second time. USD/JPY is 154.886, up 0.35%, with the weekly now +0.59%, so the yen has underperformed for a third consecutive session. Yesterday that pattern was worth a cut from +3 to +2 and it was taken. Doing it again today would be flipping on noise, and there are three specific reasons not to: the move is a 0.35% Asian session, not a full G10 session; the BoJ decides in under 72 hours with TE carrying consensus AND forecast at 1.25%, the highest policy rate since roughly September 1995, with a 97% Reuters poll behind it and overnight index swaps implying about 75 basis points of cumulative hikes by April 2027; and USD/JPY at 154.886 is back inside the zone where officials actually bought yen ten days ago, with the Takaichi administration openly opposed to further depreciation and BoJ board member Takata arguing publicly the bank should hike 'nimbly'. An intervention put under a currency three days from its highest policy rate in thirty years is not a currency to short twice in two days. USD/JPY stays RANGE. Third, China half-answered yesterday's question and the half it answered was the half that mattered. Industrial production BEAT at 5.2% against a 4.8% consensus and 4.5% previously; retail sales MISSED at 0.4% against 0.8% and 0.6% previously; fixed asset investment was in line at -7.2% and the unemployment rate ticked up to 5.3%. Copper's answer was literally a tie: 6.3303 USD per pound, 0.00% on the day, after -6.06% on the week. The file's stated trigger was a miss on BOTH prints, and that was not met, so AUD holds +1 exactly as written and the second tripwire - Australia's August labour force report on September 24 at 01:30Z, employment expected +15.1K after -15.8K - remains the live one. But XCU/USD must be corrected: yesterday it was moved from RANGE to SHORT on the strength of the weekly collapse, and the single event named as deciding it has now come in on the industrial side and the metal stopped falling dead. It goes back to RANGE. The distinction worth keeping is that the beat came in the production half, which is what copper actually consumes, while the miss came in the consumption half, which is why the AUD case is weakened without the copper case being confirmed. Fourth, the haven complex is showing its first crack in four sessions and it argues for patience rather than pressing. Gold is 4292.51, down only 0.15%, on the day the 10-year broke 5% - the single most hostile real-rate event of the month - and it is holding the 4,300 area it was squeezed toward. Silver is 63.046, down 0.29%. Compare that with Monday's -1.74% and -2.19% on softer yields. A metal that falls 2% on a war headline and 0.15% on a 19-year high in long yields is a metal whose sellers are getting tired. The XAU and XAG shorts stay on because the direction is right and the weekly numbers are -1.43% and -4.10%, but conviction stays MEDIUM and neither should be added to here. The same logic keeps CHF at zero rather than negative: the franc was second-best G10 overnight at -0.10%. Fifth, the energy leg is still working and it is now the cleanest thing on the board. WTI is 103.333, up another 1.92% with the week at +11.07% and the month at +22.29%; Brent is 107.545, +1.76%, +9.83% weekly. Brent traded above 110 intraday Monday before settling back. Heating oil is +1.98% and +10.73% on the week, gasoline +2.02%. European gas keeps grinding: EU gas 82.80 euros, +34.12% on the month; German gas 83.57, up 3.62% TODAY and +34.07% monthly; UK gas +35.09% monthly. Petroline remains shut with no restart timeline published by Riyadh, satellite imagery now showing the damage, and the Salalah meeting still postponed with no new date. USOIL stays LONG at HIGH, GER40 stays SHORT and is upgraded to MEDIUM because a 5% US 10-year is a second, independent headwind on top of the gas bill, and CAD's advantage continues to express itself through the crosses rather than against the dollar - the Canadian dollar was the BEST G10 performer overnight at -0.08%, which is exactly the relative-not-absolute claim this file corrected itself to yesterday. Sixth, sterling is the one currency whose distribution resolves within the hour. GBP/USD is 1.34818, down 0.13%, after testing five-week lows on Monday. At 06:00Z: unemployment expected to RISE to 5.0% from 4.9%, average earnings including bonus expected to FALL to 3.9% from 4.1% with TE forecasting 4.0%, earnings excluding bonus 3.5% with TE at 3.4%, employment change +70K from +83K. One correction to yesterday's file on the claimant count: TE's forecast is +5.0K against a consensus of +8.3K and a previous of -11K - not the -5,000 stated yesterday - so the split is narrower than described, though still a two-way print, with HMRC payrolls forecast at -4.0K. Then UK CPI tomorrow at 06:00Z, expected to rise to 3.1% with core 2.7% though TE's own core forecast is 2.6%, and the BoE Thursday at 11:00Z with TE carrying 3.75% and a 0/9 cut, 3/9 hike, 6/9 unchanged consensus. Sterling holds at zero into that and there is no edge taking it either way. So the book into the FOMC: keep NZD/USD, USD/CHF, NZD/JPY and USOIL as the four cleanest expressions, hold the dollar longs but do not add to them ahead of a dot plot that is now more likely to disappoint than to confirm, stand flat USD/JPY through Friday, take XCU back to RANGE, and treat a fall in US real yields - not a peace headline - as the event that unwinds this entire page at once.

geopolitics: The war has stopped being a headline risk and become a yield curve. The single most important development of the last 24 hours is that the US 10-year Treasury yield topped 5% for the first time since 2023 and closed at its highest level since 2007, and the driver was explicitly energy rather than growth: AAA has the US national average for regular gasoline at 4.31 dollars a gallon and diesel at a RECORD 6.23 dollars, and diesel is the input cost for trucking, rail, farming and shipping, so the bond market is repricing the pass-through of the shock rather than the shock itself. That is the mechanism this file has been describing in fragments for a week, and naming it changes what to watch. On the physical side nothing has improved. Saudi Arabia's East-West Crude Oil Pipeline - Petroline, 1,200 kilometres from the Eastern Province to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, carrying roughly 5 million barrels a day of crude that would otherwise transit the Gulf - remains shut after the drone strikes launched from Iraqi territory on September 10 and 11, with satellite imagery now showing the extent of the damage and Riyadh publishing no restart timeline; prediction markets are quoting odds on a restart by September 30. Petroline IS the bypass, the physical answer to a closed Hormuz, so with it offline there is no workaround left and traders have said Yanbu's stored volumes cover only five to seven days of exports. On the diplomatic side the door is still shut: the Salalah meeting between Iran and Gulf states on Oman's reopening plan remains postponed with no new date, Omani Foreign Minister Badr Albusaidi having cited 'the interests of consensus' hours after the strike near Qeshm Island that killed one and injured four aboard an Iranian commercial vessel. Tehran continues to deny direct talks with Washington, insisting its channel runs through Muscat, and the underlying dispute is unchanged - Oman's July proposal to split control of the strait 50-50 with voluntary transit fees was rejected by Tehran, which wants compulsory fees and the lifting of the US naval blockade of Iranian ports first. Hormuz traffic remains roughly 90% below pre-war levels against about 20 million barrels a day before February 28, and Houthi advances toward a second regional waterway add a parallel supply risk. Trump is pushing to restore flows ahead of November's midterms, which remains simultaneously the strongest de-escalation force on this board and the reason a sudden deal headline is a live tail risk against every position here. The price action overnight: WTI 103.333, up 1.92%, with the week at +11.07% and the month at +22.29%; Brent 107.545, +1.76%, having traded above 110 intraday Monday before settling back; heating oil +1.98% and +10.73% on the week; gasoline +2.02%. European gas keeps grinding higher with German gas up 3.62% overnight to 83.57 euros and +34.07% on the month, EU gas 82.80 at +34.12%, UK gas +35.09%. But the haven side showed its first crack in four sessions and it matters: gold fell only 0.15% to 4292.51 on the day the 10-year broke 5%, against -1.74% on Monday's softer-yield session, and silver fell only 0.29% against -2.19%. A metal that drops 2% on a war headline and 0.15% on a 19-year high in long yields has sellers who are running out of conviction. The demand-side counterweight also still makes the crude rally fragile rather than structural: the IEA cut its 2026 global demand forecast to a DECLINE of 2.5 million barrels a day from 1.6 million, OPEC cut demand growth for a fifth consecutive month and the EIA still projects Brent near 90 dollars in H2 on a gradual Hormuz recovery. Practically: hold USOIL LONG while the bypass is shut but treat it as headline-fragile; keep the CHF crosses long and XAU and XAG short without adding to them, because the confirming evidence stopped overnight; express Canada's energy advantage through EUR/CAD, AUD/CAD, NZD/CAD and GBP/CAD rather than against the dollar, since a frozen BoC cannot beat an 89%-priced Fed hike; short the energy importers of this shock through GER40 - now a MEDIUM short, squeezed by a 5% US 10-year as well as by gas - and through the kiwi. And keep the real invalidation in view: this whole page is short US real yields staying high, and Wednesday's dot plot is the event that tests it.
